label: Morning edition
summary: Keanu, **September CPI hit 3.7%** on Wednesday, hotter than the 3.6% economists expected, with gasoline up 9.1% on the month and the 10-year yield jumping to about 5.31% (CNBC, CNN, Fox Business). The Fed meets Oct. 28 and markets expect a pause, then a hike in December (CNBC). In Washington, **a bipartisan group of senators called Trump's Russian diesel deal a betrayal**, with an Oct. 18 sanctions deadline ahead (Axios, Fox News, CNN). Federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's home Monday in a criminal probe, and Democrats and Trump allies split sharply over the timing (NPR, Fox News, The Hill). The Senate debates in Georgia, Maine and Iowa put Trump on the ballot, and Iowa's Ashley Hinson broke with him on the diesel deal (CNN, The Hill). In the Gulf, **a Houthi strike hit a Saudi Aramco building** while Riyadh's airport stays shut through Oct. 17 (CNBC, Fox News, CNN). Closer to home, **California's Prop. 40 billionaire tax leads 52-46** but could be voided by Props. 41 or 42 (CalMatters, KQED), and a Bay Area transit tax faces a lawsuit over its ballot wording (KQED). On the tech side, **Microsoft says it will mainly use its Maia 300 chip** for AI inference, and Meta launched its first frontier model, Muse Wonder (CNBC, Axios, TechCrunch). NASA's Artemis II data release includes five faint impact flashes spotted by the crew (NASA, Space.com). Expect a hot Friday in Fremont, with a high of 92.

alerts.text: September CPI came in at 3.7%, above forecasts, and 10-year yields jumped to about 5.31%. The Fed meets Oct. 28.
Fremont heats up Friday, Oct. 16, with a high of 92 and a low of 65, then 88 on Saturday.
Oct. 18 is the White House deadline to begin implementing the Graham Russia sanctions law, with the diesel deal fight in play.
Tesla reports Oct. 21 after the close, the first of your six watchlist names to report.

highlights.text: September CPI hit 3.7%, hotter than expected, as gasoline jumped 9.1% and Treasury yields surged.
Bipartisan senators call Trump's Russian diesel deal a betrayal ahead of an Oct. 18 sanctions deadline.
A Houthi strike hits a Saudi Aramco building as Trump pauses Iran strikes until after the midterms.
California's billionaire tax leads 52-46, but Brin-backed Props. 41 and 42 could cancel it.
Microsoft's Maia 300 chip will handle most of its AI inference, with deployments starting in 2027.

stat.label: U.S. inflation, September, year over year
stat.note: Up from forecasts of 3.6%; gasoline is up 34.2% on the year (CNBC)

markets.wrap: Stocks ended Tuesday nearly flat, with the **S&P 500 at 7,805.45** and the Dow down 0.35%, as memory-chip names fell for a second day and Micron lost about 3.6% on Chinese competition fears (CNBC). The CPI report then pushed **the 10-year Treasury yield to about 5.31%** and futures lower (CNBC). Crude oil stays elevated after Houthi and Iranian attacks, with Brent at $106.65 on Monday (CNBC). Banks reported mixed third-quarter results (CNBC).

stories.title: Bipartisan letter calls Trump's Russian diesel deal a betrayal as an Oct. 18 sanctions deadline nears
stories.summary: Senators from both parties urge Trump to scrap the Treasury license, while analysts doubt the deal will cut U.S. diesel prices.
story: A bipartisan group of senators sent Trump a letter calling his Russian diesel deal a "betrayal" of Ukraine and urging him to withdraw, Axios and Fox News report. Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis are among the critics. They say a 2022 law bars Russian energy imports and that the administration did not consult Congress. Outlets differ on the count of signers, six or seven in some accounts.

Treasury's General License No. 135 lets Russian-origin diesel be sold, delivered and imported through April 7, 2027, Fox News reports. Trump said the deal would put more than 300,000 tons on the world market right away and defended it as a way to ease prices. CNBC reports analysts see little price relief, and Sen. John Barrasso has called it leverage against Putin, Fox News reports.

The next test is Oct. 18, when the White House faces a deadline to begin implementing the newer sanctions law named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. The law lets the president waive key provisions, which is the crux of the dispute (Axios, CNBC). Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a Pennsylvania Republican, says he will introduce a bill to block Russian oil purchases and seek a discharge petition, with Rep. Don Bacon as a cosponsor (The Hill, Fox News).
Not every Republican objects. Rep. Thomas Massie voiced support for the diesel decision, the Washington Examiner reports. Treasury says it is acting in compliance with all applicable laws.
stories.flag: Reports differ on the number of senators who signed. I found no report that Fitzpatrick has filed his discharge petition.
facts: Treasury's license allows Russian diesel imports through April 7, 2027 (Fox News).
Collins, Murkowski, Tillis and Curtis are among the Republican critics (Fox News, Axios).
Oct. 18 is the deadline to begin implementing the Graham sanctions law, which allows waivers (Axios, CNBC).
Trump said more than 300,000 tons would flow immediately (Fox News).
Treasury says the license complies with applicable laws (Axios).
stories.left: Democrats say the deal rewards Putin while he strikes Ukraine's grid, and that it breaks a law Congress passed with large bipartisan majorities. They point to Republican senators who agree it may be illegal, and argue it was timed to lower fuel prices before the midterms at Kyiv's expense. They want Congress to force a vote and the sanctions law fully enforced.
stories.right: Supporters argue the world diesel market is tight, and that putting more barrels on it helps drivers and farmers while it does little for Moscow. Allies like Barrasso frame it as leverage Trump can pull back if Putin stalls. Conservative critics, including Collins and Tillis, say the plainer reading of the 2022 law bars it, and that any waiver should go through Congress.
stories.next: Oct. 18 is the Graham sanctions deadline. Watch for a Fitzpatrick petition filing and any Treasury change to the license.

stories.title: Federal agents search Rep. Ilhan Omar's home in a criminal investigation, weeks before the midterms
stories.summary: Homeland Security Investigations executed a court-authorized warrant Monday, and no charges have been announced.
story: Federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington-area home early Monday, Oct. 12. The Justice Department said Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant as part of an ongoing criminal investigation. It did not name Omar, according to NPR, NBC News and CNN. No charges have been announced.

Fox News and National Review report, citing sources, that the probe concerns immigration fraud involving paperwork her father filled out when she was a child. Omar is a U.S. citizen and has denied past fraud allegations. She called the search an attempt to "target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement." Fox says border czar Tom Homan had confirmed a criminal investigation about a month earlier.

Democratic leaders called the search deeply disturbing, many objected to the timing three weeks before the election, and The Hill reports Rep. Don Beyer called it "insanely corrupt even for Donald Trump." Trump said he had "nothing to do with it" and called Omar "totally crooked" (The Hill, Washington Examiner). A former prosecutor told Fox News the unwritten 60-day rule Democrats cite is a norm, not a ban.
The Washington Examiner reports Omar has begun fundraising off the search. The affidavit that won the warrant is not public, so the strength of the case is unknown.
stories.flag: Details of the alleged immigration-fraud theory come from unnamed sources cited by Fox News, Reuters and National Review. The Justice Department has not described the investigation.
facts: Agents searched Omar's home on Monday, Oct. 12 under a court-authorized warrant (NPR, NBC News).
The Justice Department confirmed an ongoing criminal investigation but did not name Omar (NPR).
No charges have been announced (The Hill).
Omar denies wrongdoing and calls the search political (CNN, Washington Examiner).
Trump says he had "nothing to do with it" (Washington Examiner).
stories.left: Democrats see a president using federal agents against a prominent critic weeks before voters decide. They cite the unwritten norm against overt investigative steps near an election, and Omar's status as a naturalized citizen and refugee, as reasons for suspicion. Without charges or a public affidavit, they say the public cannot tell law enforcement from retaliation.
stories.right: Conservatives say a judge approved a warrant, and that credible allegations of immigration fraud by a member of Congress deserve investigation whatever the calendar says. They note the 60-day idea is an informal norm, and that Democrats cannot claim immunity from scrutiny. They also point out that Trump denies involvement and that the career agency, not the White House, executed the search.
stories.next: Watch for charges, a court unsealing of the affidavit, or House action. The election is Nov. 3.

stories.title: Senate debates in Georgia, Maine and Iowa turn on Trump, Epstein and the Russia diesel deal
stories.summary: Iowa's Ashley Hinson broke with Trump on the diesel deal, while Georgia's Ossoff and Collins clashed over Epstein files and 2020.
story: Three Senate debates on Tuesday, Oct. 13, put Trump on the ballot without him on stage, CNN reports. In Iowa's final debate, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson said "We need to lower diesel prices, but I don't think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it." Democrat Josh Turek said it was a rare point of agreement, The Hill reports. Hinson also backed a quick end to the Iran war but balked when asked whether she would again vote against a war powers resolution.

In Georgia, Sen. Jon Ossoff and Rep. Mike Collins clashed over Epstein. Collins linked Ossoff to donor Reid Hoffman, who has said he met Epstein, and Ossoff noted Collins's earlier opposition to releasing the files, though Collins later joined the near-unanimous House vote for the Epstein Files Transparency Act (The Hill). Collins also would not say Trump won in 2020, answering that Joe Biden was the president. Ossoff said he has "zero interest" in running for president in 2028 (NBC News, The Hill).

In Maine, Sen. Susan Collins said she has voted to rein in Trump's war powers after the Iran conflict passed 60 days, and she faced Democrat Troy Jackson on energy costs (CNN). The Washington Examiner reports a Democratic super PAC has pulled Ossoff ads from Georgia as a sign of confidence. An Iowa poll cited by The Hill has Hinson at 47% and Turek at 45%, and Cook rates the race a toss-up.
Trump spent the night at a rally in Alaska. With three weeks to go, affordability and the Iran war are the common thread in all three races.
stories.flag: The Iowa poll is a single survey cited by The Hill. Maine debate detail comes mostly from CNN.
facts: Hinson said she opposes making a deal with Russia to lower diesel prices (The Hill).
Ossoff said he has zero interest in running for president and will serve a full term (NBC News, The Hill).
Mike Collins said Joe Biden was president and avoided saying Trump won 2020 (The Hill).
Susan Collins says she voted to rein in war powers after the Iran war passed 60 days (CNN).
The Iowa race is rated a toss-up by Cook (The Hill).
stories.left: Democrats say these debates show Republicans tied to an unpopular president on prices, the Iran war and tariffs, and that candidates like Hinson only break with him when it is safe. They argue Collins's 2020 answer and the Epstein exchange show who will stand up to Trump. Ossoff's team points to polling and a PAC ad pullback as evidence the map is shifting.
stories.right: Republicans say Democrats are running on personal attacks and that their candidates are talking about gas prices, border security and the economy. Hinson's break on Russia shows independence, they argue, and Collins's Epstein-vote record shows he backed transparency. They note Iowa and Maine remain competitive for the GOP and that debate moments rarely move voters this late.
stories.next: Early voting and mail ballots are underway, and Election Day is Nov. 3. Watch new Georgia and Iowa polls.

stories.title: Prop. 40 billionaire tax leads narrowly while Brin-backed rivals could cancel it
stories.summary: PPIC has the one-time 5% tax at 52-46, but Props. 41 and 42 poll higher and Newsom backs one of them.
story: California's Prop. 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on billionaires to fund health care and education (KQED). A September PPIC poll found 52% of likely voters in favor and 46% opposed, a statistical tie given the margin of error, CalMatters reports. KQED notes support in the low to mid 50s is short of the roughly 60% backers usually want before a well-funded opposition campaign.

The bigger risk is Props. 41 and 42. They contain language that would void conflicting measures that get fewer votes, so Prop. 40 could pass and still be canceled. In the same PPIC poll Prop. 41 had 51% and Prop. 42 had 54%. Gov. Gavin Newsom opposes Prop. 40 and endorsed Prop. 42, CalMatters reports.

Money is lopsided. CalMatters says Google co-founder Sergey Brin has put more than $138 million into the opposition, and that opponents have raised more than $205 million. The San Francisco Chronicle reports the state Democratic Party and the California Labor Federation endorsed the tax while San Francisco Democrats voted to oppose it, which shows the split inside the party.
For the Bay Area, the stakes include state funding for schools and health care and the future of Silicon Valley founders' wealth in California. The election is Nov. 3.
stories.flag: Fundraising totals vary by outlet and date. The Chronicle and KQED cite lower figures for Brin and the main PAC.
facts: Prop. 40 is a one-time 5% tax on billionaires (KQED).
PPIC (Sept. 4-10) had 52% yes and 46% no (CalMatters).
Props. 41 and 42 would void conflicting measures with fewer votes (CalMatters).
Newsom opposes Prop. 40 and endorsed Prop. 42 (CalMatters).
Brin has given more than $138 million to the opposition, per CalMatters.
stories.left: Supporters say a small group of the very rich can afford a one-time levy, and that the money would fund health care and schools while federal cuts bite. They argue the opposition's $200 million is proof of how much the wealthy fear paying, and that Props. 41 and 42 are a trick to nullify a majority vote.
stories.right: Opponents argue a wealth tax can push founders and capital out of California, and that a one-time tax invites repeat ones. They say the state already collects record income-tax revenue from the wealthy and should fix spending first. Even some Democrats, including Newsom, say the tax is the wrong tool and back Props. 41 and 42 as a safeguard.
stories.next: Ballots are out and the election is Nov. 3. Watch the next PPIC and Berkeley IGS polls.

stories.title: Bay Area transit sales tax heads to November ballot as voters sue over its wording
stories.summary: A half-cent tax in four counties and one cent in San Francisco would raise about $14 billion over 14 years for BART, Caltrain and others.
story: The Connect Bay Area measure will be on the Nov. 3 ballot in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, Santa Clara and San Francisco counties after backers submitted more than 305,000 signatures, well over the 186,000 needed, Contra Costa News and Mass Transit report. Because it came from signatures, it needs only a simple majority.

KQED reports the tax would be 0.5% in four counties and 1% in San Francisco and raise about $14 billion over 14 years, roughly $1.2 billion a year, mostly for BART, Caltrain, Muni and AC Transit. The campaign says without it BART could see up to 15 station closures and service cuts of up to 70%, and Caltrain would run hourly with no weekend service. Those are the campaign's projections.

Ten Bay Area voters sued in Santa Clara County Superior Court, arguing the ballot question is deceptive and biased toward yes, KQED reports. They say it stresses service cuts if the tax fails and that MTC's revenue estimate is about $200 million a year too low. I found no ruling in the results.
For Fremont, the measure matters because BART's Fremont line and the Warm Springs extension depend on regional operating money.
stories.flag: I did not find the court's ruling or the final ballot wording. Service-cut figures are campaign projections.
facts: The tax is 0.5% in four counties and 1% in San Francisco (KQED).
It would raise about $14 billion over 14 years (KQED).
Backers filed more than 305,000 signatures against 186,000 needed (Contra Costa News).
It needs a simple majority because it is a citizen initiative (Mass Transit).
Ten voters sued over the ballot wording (KQED).
stories.left: Supporters say the region cannot let BART, Caltrain and Muni shrink, since cuts push riders into cars, hurt low-income workers and undo climate goals. They argue a sales tax shared across five counties is the fairest way to avoid the death spiral and that the signatures show strong public support.
stories.right: Critics say the ballot language is slanted and that agencies should show reforms and cost control before asking for more money. A sales tax hits lower-income shoppers, they argue, and a $14 billion take with no firm performance targets invites waste. Some also object to the simple-majority route that avoids a two-thirds vote.
stories.next: The lawsuit decision and Nov. 3 vote are next. Watch for MTC and county registrar updates.

stories.title: Houthi missiles hit a Saudi Aramco building as Trump holds off on Iran strikes until after the midterms
stories.summary: Riyadh's airport stays closed through Oct. 17, Iran attacks ships near Hormuz, and Brent crude sits above $100.
story: Saudi officials said an administrative building belonging to Saudi Aramco was targeted overnight, CNBC reports, and CNN says the Houthis and Saudi Arabia traded fresh strikes. Accounts of the damage differ. CNN reports Saudi authorities described a limited fire, while Fox News cites Reuters sources reporting extensive damage at the Dhahran headquarters. Reuters also reported operations continued normally.

Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport remains shut through Oct. 17 after Saturday's Houthi strike, Fox News reports. Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the Nov. 3 midterms, CNBC reports, and said the Houthis are probably acting at Iran's behest to drive up oil prices before the election.

At sea, Fox News counts 10 attacks on ships this week, six Sunday and four Tuesday, and the IRGC claimed a commercial ship hit a mine. CNBC quotes the IRGC chief saying Tehran is "counting the moments" until it can attack U.S. warships, while CENTCOM says U.S. and partner forces control the strait. Brent crude closed at $106.65 on Monday, CNBC reports.
WTI trades near $95 this morning, up about 1.4% (live market data). Oil has fed directly into the 3.7% inflation print.
stories.flag: The extent of damage to Aramco's Dhahran site is disputed between CNN and Fox News (citing Reuters).
facts: Trump said U.S. forces will not attack Iran before the Nov. 3 midterms (CNBC).
Riyadh airport is closed through Oct. 17 (Fox News).
Saudi officials said an Aramco administrative building was targeted overnight (CNBC).
Fox News counts 10 ship attacks near Hormuz this week.
Brent closed at $106.65 on Monday (CNBC).
stories.left: Democrats say the war has cost the average household about $2,000 according to Moody's, per The Hill, and that Congress never authorized an open-ended conflict. They argue the Gulf escalation shows the war is widening, and that Trump's midterm pause treats strikes as a campaign decision instead of a strategic one.
stories.right: Conservatives argue Iran and its Houthi proxies are the aggressors, and that attacks on Saudi airports and shipping lanes show why Tehran cannot be allowed to control Hormuz. Many back firm U.S. support for Riyadh and deterrence against Iran, and see the Houthi surge as the cost of earlier restraint. Some on the right worry about open-ended entanglement.
stories.next: Riyadh airport reopens no earlier than Oct. 17. Watch for a decision on U.S. action against the Houthis.

stories.title: Zelenskyy says Washington warned it could cut intelligence sharing over strikes on Russian refineries
stories.summary: Trump's announced "energy ceasefire" has not been formally accepted by either side, and Russia still hit Ukrainian transport and logistics.
story: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told NPR the Trump administration warned it could cut off intelligence sharing unless Ukraine stops long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries. The White House did not confirm the threat, and Trump said "We are helping them and we are sharing intel," NPR reports. CNN and others have reported similar warnings from European officials.

On Sunday Trump announced an immediate "energy ceasefire" and said both sides agreed. Zelenskyy said he learned of it from social media and was awaiting details, and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was opaque, saying contacts continue, CNBC reports. Zelenskyy said Russia hit six Ukrainian energy sites that day.

NPR reports Russia hit no Ukrainian energy targets overnight for the first time since the announcement, but struck transport and logistics with ballistic missiles and drones. Zelenskyy said Ukraine has not hit Russian refineries since Sunday and would keep stopping if Moscow stops striking the grid.
The pressure links to the diesel deal. Critics tie the U.S. push for lower fuel prices to the pressure on Kyiv, CNN reports.
stories.flag: The intelligence-cutoff threat rests on Zelenskyy and unnamed European officials. The White House did not confirm it.
facts: Zelenskyy told NPR the U.S. warned it could cut intelligence sharing (NPR).
Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" on Sunday, Oct. 11 (Axios, CNBC).
Neither Moscow nor Kyiv has formally accepted it (CNBC).
Russia hit no Ukrainian energy targets overnight but struck transport and logistics (NPR).
Zelenskyy said Ukraine has paused refinery strikes since Sunday (NPR).
stories.left: Critics say the administration is pressuring the victim while easing sanctions on the aggressor, and that threatening intelligence sharing risks Ukrainian lives. They see a ceasefire announced by social media, without Kyiv or Moscow signing on, as a stunt tied to U.S. fuel prices.
stories.right: Supporters say Trump is trying to end a stalemate and cool oil prices that hurt Americans and allies. They argue refinery strikes raise global fuel costs and risk escalation, and that U.S. aid should come with leverage. Hawks in the party counter that pressuring Kyiv while easing Moscow is the wrong order.
stories.next: Watch whether Moscow publicly accepts the ceasefire and whether Washington acts on the intelligence warning.

stories.title: September inflation rises to 3.7% as gasoline jumps 9.1% in a month
stories.summary: Consumer prices rose 0.6% in September and 3.7% from a year earlier, above forecasts, with gasoline driving about half the monthly gain.
story: The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Wednesday that the consumer price index rose 0.6% in September and 3.7% from a year earlier. Economists had expected 3.6% on the year, so the annual figure came in hotter than forecast while the monthly gain matched expectations (CNBC, CNN, Fox Business). Gasoline jumped 9.1% in the month and made up about half of the headline increase. It is up 34.2% over the past year, CNBC reports.

Core CPI, which leaves out food and energy, rose 0.3% on the month and 2.6% on the year. Forecasters had looked for 0.2% and 2.5%, CNBC reports. The Fed raised rates a quarter point in September, 12-0, to a range of 3.75% to 4%. CNBC says markets now expect the central bank to skip a hike at its Oct. 28 meeting and raise again in December.

Bond traders reacted fast. The 10-year Treasury yield jumped to about 5.31% after the release and the 30-year to about 5.56%, and stock futures turned lower, according to CNBC. The Fed's preferred inflation gauge is PCE, and Deutsche Bank analysts noted that September's PCE arrives after the next rate decision.
For households, the energy shock matters more than the core figure. The headline number is the one drivers see at the pump, and it lands three weeks before the Nov. 3 midterms.
stories.flag: Fed pricing comes from a single CNBC report, and fed funds futures had not moved much right after the release.
facts: Headline CPI rose 0.6% in September and 3.7% year over year (CNBC, CNN).
Economists expected 3.6% on the year, per CNBC.
Gasoline rose 9.1% on the month, about half the headline gain, and is up 34.2% on the year (CNBC).
Core CPI rose 0.3% on the month and 2.6% on the year, slightly above forecasts (CNBC).
The 10-year Treasury yield jumped to about 5.31% after the report (CNBC).
stories.left: Progressives say this is a bill for choices the administration made. The Iran war and the tariffs both raise costs, and Moody's estimated the war costs the average household about $2,000, as The Hill reported. They argue the White House cannot call the economy strong while gas is up a third in a year, and that the Fed is now raising rates on top of a supply shock the president could ease by ending the war.
stories.right: Conservatives say the energy spike traces to Iran's attacks on shipping and its proxies, and that core inflation at 2.6% shows the underlying economy is not overheating. They argue the answer is more domestic production and a firm line on Iran, not blaming tariffs for a gasoline shock. They also note the Fed has already moved, and that a one-month energy jump can reverse if Hormuz traffic improves.
stories.next: The Fed meets Oct. 28, with PCE inflation due later this month and the Nov. 3 midterms days after.

stories.title: Memory stocks slide for a second day and Treasury yields jump on hot inflation
stories.summary: Micron fell about 3.6% Tuesday on Chinese competition fears, and the 10-year yield rose to roughly 5.31% after the CPI report.
story: Wall Street ended Tuesday slightly lower. The Dow fell 180.45 points, or 0.35%, to 51,670.10, the S&P 500 slipped 0.02% to 7,805.45 and the Nasdaq lost 0.15% to 27,204.38, CNBC reports. Memory-chip stocks fell for a second day, with Micron down about 3.6% as investors weighed competition from China's CXMT, which reported progress on a new chip structure (CNBC).
Big banks added to the mix. JPMorgan and Wells Fargo reported mixed third-quarter results, CNBC reports, and closing moves were reported differently across sources.

Wednesday's CPI report moved rates. The 10-year Treasury yield jumped to about 5.31% and the 30-year to about 5.56%, and stock futures slipped, CNBC reports. Bloomberg reported Tuesday that Treasuries gained on haven demand when trading resumed after the holiday, with the 10-year sliding to about 5.19%.
Among your names, Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet were up slightly at last report and Tesla and Amazon were down, all well under 2%.
stories.flag: Bank closing moves for JPMorgan and Wells Fargo varied between sources, so I left them out.
facts: S&P 500 closed at 7,805.45, down 0.02% (CNBC).
Micron fell about 3.6% Tuesday (CNBC).
The 10-year yield rose to about 5.31% after the CPI report (CNBC).
CNBC links the selloff to progress at China's CXMT, a rival to Micron and Korean memory makers.
Tesla reports Oct. 21 after the close.
stories.why: Higher yields raise discount rates on long-duration tech, while memory makers face a pricing challenge from a state-backed Chinese rival. Among your names, Microsoft's push into its own chips is the thing to watch for Nvidia, and Tesla reports next week.
stories.next: Tesla reports Oct. 21 after the close. Alphabet and Microsoft follow Oct. 28.

stories.title: Microsoft unveils Maia 300 and says it will mainly use its own chips for inference
stories.summary: The third-generation accelerator claims 40% more tokens per megawatt than GPU systems, with multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027.
story: Microsoft unveiled its third-generation Maia accelerator, Maia 300, on Monday, Oct. 12, and said it will mainly use its own silicon to handle incoming AI requests, CNBC reports. Microsoft says the chip runs about 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems. These are company claims with no independent benchmarks yet.

CNBC says a rack holds 96 Maia 300 chips, double the Maia 200 count. Production starts in 2027, and Microsoft is aiming for multi-gigawatt scale, but a Microsoft general manager declined to give a timeline (CNBC, Axios). One report says the chip uses TSMC's N2P process with HBM4 memory.

Limits matter. Nvidia and AMD remain Microsoft's partners for training, and Axios reports the push applies to Microsoft's own services, not necessarily to Azure customers like OpenAI. Evercore ISI estimates Maia will be about 10% of Microsoft's AI chip spending by the first quarter of 2027, CNBC reports.
Axios frames it as part of a wider trend in which every major Nvidia customer is now building a competing chip.
stories.flag: The process node and HBM4 details come from a single secondary report, and performance numbers are Microsoft's own.
facts: Microsoft unveiled Maia 300 on Oct. 12 (CNBC).
It claims about 40% more tokens per megawatt than GPU systems (CNBC).
A rack holds 96 chips (CNBC).
Production starts in 2027 (CNBC).
Evercore ISI sees Maia at about 10% of Microsoft's AI chip spend by Q1 2027 (CNBC).
stories.why: Inference is the largest recurring cost in AI. If hyperscalers serve most requests on their own chips, Nvidia's share of that demand shrinks even as training demand stays strong, and it changes how AI hardware gets designed around power limits.
stories.next: Watch Microsoft's Oct. 28 earnings for capex and Maia deployment commentary.

stories.title: How Delhi cut electricity losses from about 50% to about 5%
stories.summary: IEEE Spectrum says metering, private distribution and regulation, not one technology, drove the 25-year turnaround.
story: Delhi cut the share of electricity lost to technical problems and theft from about 50% to about 5% over roughly 25 years, according to an IEEE Spectrum feature by electrical engineer Mini Shaji Thomas. The October issue lists the story as a cover item. The article stresses that technology alone did not do it.

Reform began with a 2002 restructuring of the Delhi Vidyut Board's distribution business, which split the city among private utilities, Spectrum reports. Tata Power-DDL took over north and northwest Delhi, and BSES runs the rest through two companies. Early steps included swapping electromechanical meters for electronic ones and upgrading cables in high-theft areas.

Hackaday summarized the piece and noted theft was widespread among both powerful and poor customers. Tata Power-DDL reports aggregate technical and commercial losses of 5.42% in fiscal 2025-26, while a US Energy Association case study puts it below 6.39%, so exact figures vary by source.
The lesson for other grids is that regulation, investment and enforcement had to move together.
stories.flag: I only saw excerpts of the Spectrum article. Exact loss figures differ slightly by source.
facts: Delhi's losses fell from about 50% to about 5% (IEEE Spectrum).
The reform began with a 2002 restructuring that split distribution among private utilities (IEEE Spectrum).
Early steps included electronic meters and cable upgrades (IEEE Spectrum).
Tata Power-DDL reports 5.42% losses for fiscal 2025-26 (company figure).
The author is Mini Shaji Thomas of Jamia Millia Islamia (IEEE Spectrum).
stories.why: Grid losses waste generation that has already been paid for. As demand from data centers and electrification rises, cutting losses is one of the cheapest ways to add usable power, and Delhi shows it takes governance as much as hardware.
stories.next: Watch whether other Indian states and utilities copy the model.

stories.title: NASA releases 800 GB of Artemis II lunar data, including five faint impact flashes
stories.summary: The crew's handheld images and audio form the first mainly human-collected planetary dataset in more than 50 years, NASA says.
story: NASA released more than 800 gigabytes of Artemis II lunar science data on Oct. 7 through its Planetary Data System, the agency says. The set includes more than 11,000 full-resolution images and video from the crew's handheld cameras and Orion's cameras, and 8.5 hours of crew audio describing what they saw (NASA, AIAA).

Astronauts saw five very faint impact flashes on the Moon near the far side from about 74,000 kilometers away while Orion was behind the Moon during a planned communications break, according to coverage of the release (Space.com). Crew notes also describe lunar colors, the day-night terminator and craters and old lava flows.

NASA calls it the first planetary science dataset captured mainly by humans in more than half a century, and says it already informs Artemis III planning. The agency also published a preliminary science report, an observational report and a user guide, and says more papers are coming.
NASA reports it has finished stacking the Artemis III boosters and plans a tanking test at Pad 39B in the coming months.
stories.flag: The flashes are crew observations. I found no peer-reviewed analysis yet, and NASA calls the reports preliminary.
facts: NASA released over 800 GB of Artemis II science data on Oct. 7 (NASA).
The release holds over 11,000 images and video and 8.5 hours of audio (AIAA).
Crew saw five faint impact flashes (Space.com).
NASA published a preliminary science report and a data guide (NASA).
Artemis III booster stacking is complete (NASA).
stories.why: Human eyes caught flashes that instruments might miss, and the dataset gives researchers a baseline for choosing Artemis III science targets and for sizing the lunar impact rate that future crews and hardware will face.
stories.next: Watch for peer-reviewed papers on the impact flashes and the Artemis III tanking test at Pad 39B.

stories.title: Hubble archive data points to a possible second-generation planet around a white dwarf
stories.summary: Niobium in the white dwarf HS 0209+0832 suggests a gas giant formed from material the dying star shed, NASA says.
story: A Nature Astronomy paper that NASA announced Oct. 5 reports a candidate second-generation planet around the white dwarf HS 0209+0832, based on reanalysis of archival Hubble data. The paper is titled "Discovery of a second-generation planet candidate accreting onto a white dwarf."

Hubble's spectrum shows absorption from niobium, nickel and calcium. The team says niobium is a key clue because these heavy elements form in the conditions inside dying stars. They found niobium more than three orders of magnitude above the Sun's level and none in 33 other metal-polluted white dwarfs, according to coverage of the study.

The researchers propose that once the star ejected enriched material, some of it coalesced into a Jupiter-size planet. TESS data show periodic dimming consistent with a planet that is rapidly losing atmosphere. Lead author Jamie Williams said it is not confirmed and is a candidate for now.
Rival explanations such as ordinary asteroid debris falling onto the star are weaker here, the paper says, because the abundance pattern cannot be explained by direct fallback.
stories.flag: This is a candidate, not a confirmed planet. Mass and orbit details were not in the results I retrieved.
facts: NASA announced the result on Oct. 5, 2026 (NASA).
The paper appeared in Nature Astronomy (Nature Astronomy).
Hubble's spectrum shows niobium, nickel and calcium (NASA).
Niobium was found at over 1,000 times solar abundance (Sci.News).
The planet is a candidate, not confirmed (Smithsonian).
stories.why: If confirmed, it would show planets can form from a star's death throes, which changes how astronomers read the chemistry of polluted white dwarfs and expands where planetary systems can start.
stories.next: Watch for follow-up Hubble or JWST observations to confirm the planet's orbit and mass.

stories.title: Meta releases Muse Wonder, its first frontier-class model, and keeps the top version off the API
stories.summary: Meta says Wonder and Wonder Full match leading OpenAI and Anthropic models on its benchmarks, but the claims are unverified.
story: Meta released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full on Oct. 12 and called them its first frontier-class models, TechCrunch and Axios report. Meta's model card says they achieve scores comparable to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra, and Meta says Wonder beats those rivals on MemoryBench. These are Meta's own benchmarks.

Access is tiered. Standard Wonder is on Meta's API at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, and in the Muse personal agent app for $20 or $100 a month. Wonder Full, the stronger model, is limited to subscribers of the Muse Code plan and will not be served through the API, according to the coverage (CNBC, Bloomberg).

The release follows Meta's earlier open-weight push, so keeping Wonder Full closed marks a shift. CNBC frames the launch as a test of whether users will pay. Bloomberg describes a 14-month push to reach the frontier.
No independent evaluations have appeared yet.
stories.flag: All performance claims come from Meta. I found no independent benchmarks.
facts: Meta released Muse Wonder and Wonder Full on Oct. 12 (TechCrunch, Axios).
Meta's benchmarks put them comparable to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra (Meta model card via press).
Wonder costs $4 per million input and $20 per million output tokens (press reports).
Wonder Full is limited to Muse Code subscribers (CNBC).
Bloomberg describes a 14-month push to reach the frontier.
stories.why: A fourth lab claiming frontier performance adds price pressure and choice. Withholding the top model from the API shows even Meta is now guarding its best weights and compute for paying users.
stories.next: Watch for independent evals and whether developers adopt Muse Code.

stories.title: Google launches a Gemini work agent with Anthropic's Claude as its first third-party model
stories.summary: The agent works inside Workspace, Microsoft 365 and Slack, and picks a model per task by default.
story: Google Cloud launched a Gemini agent for work on Oct. 8, TechCrunch and CNBC report. By default the agent picks the model it judges best for each task, and users can choose one themselves. Anthropic's Claude is the first third-party model family offered, and Google says open-source and private models will follow.

The agent works inside Google Workspace apps such as Gmail, Docs, Sheets and Calendar, and it can also be used through Microsoft 365 and Slack, plus mobile, desktop and command-line surfaces, according to the coverage.

CNBC places the launch in an escalating race. An Oct. 2 CNBC piece asks whether Google's Gemini 4 Argon can really catch OpenAI and Anthropic, and a Sept. 6 CNBC story describes growing model fatigue as labs release new versions at a frenetic pace.
For businesses, letting an agent route across vendors reduces lock-in to one lab.
stories.flag: Exact Claude model names should be checked against Anthropic's documentation.
facts: Google launched the agent on Oct. 8 (TechCrunch, CNBC).
Claude is the first third-party model offered (TechCrunch).
It works in Workspace, Microsoft 365 and Slack (TechCrunch).
Google plans to add open-source and private models (TechCrunch).
The agent selects a model per task by default (CNBC).
stories.why: Routing across vendors turns models into interchangeable parts and moves competition to the agent layer, where tools, data access and trust matter more than a single benchmark score.
stories.next: Watch enterprise adoption numbers and which models Google adds next.
